# Tuberculosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Pulmonology > Infectious lung diseases > Tuberculosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/5h0ief)

---

## Summary

Tuberculosis (TB) is a disease caused by <u>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</u>, which typically affects the <u>lungs</u>. It is a common infectious cause of <u>morbidity</u> and mortality worldwide. Primary infection, transmitted via airborne aerosol <u>droplet nuclei</u>, is often initially asymptomatic. <u>M. tuberculosis</u> infection is typically dormant (<u>latent TB</u> infection; <u>LTBI</u>) because of intact innate and cellular <u>immune responses</u>. If the <u>immune system</u> is compromised, however, reactivation of the infection may occur and lead to <u>active TB</u>. Patients with active disease characteristically present with <u>fever</u>, weight loss, night sweats, and a productive <u>cough</u> (with or without <u>hemoptysis</u>) that does not respond to conventional <u>antibiotic therapy</u>. The infection may spread hematologically to any organ, causing <u>extrapulmonary TB</u>. However, disseminated disease is rare, occurring in severely <u>immunocompromised individuals</u>. If <u>active TB infection</u> is suspected, imaging should be obtained as well as microscopy, cultures, and/or <u>polymerase chain reaction</u> (<u>PCR</u>) to identify <u>M. tuberculosis</u>. The <u>treatment of tuberculosis</u> is prolonged due to the slow growth of <u>M. tuberculosis</u>, its concealment in <u>macrophages</u>, and the inability of drugs to easily penetrate its <u>cell wall</u>. Standard treatment includes combination therapy with <u>rifampin</u>, <u>isoniazid</u>, <u>ethambutol</u>, and <u>pyrazinamide</u> for two months, followed by <u>rifampin</u> and <u>isoniazid</u> for an additional four months. Patients with suspected <u>LTBI</u> should be tested using the purified protein derivative (<u>PPD</u>) <u>tuberculin skin test</u> (<u>TST</u>) or <u>interferon-γ release assay</u> (<u>IGRA</u>) and treated accordingly. Treatment of <u>LTBI</u> reduces the risk of active infection in up to 90% of cases and, therefore, plays a crucial role in the prevention of <u>active TB</u>.

* Active tuberculosis 

* Definition: any TB infection with symptoms and signs of disease, including <u>primary TB</u> and reactivation of <u>latent TB</u> [[1]](/library/kIYm1q)[[6]](/library/z5Yr5p)[[7]](/library/thXXfB)

* Features [[1]](/library/kIYm1q)

* Pulmonary TB: the most common form of <u>active TB</u>

* <u>Extrapulmonary TB</u>: The most common forms are <u>TB lymphadenitis</u> and <u>pleural tuberculosis</u>.

* Diagnostics: confirmed if <u>bacilli</u> are present in respiratory secretions or other tissues, and subsequent microbiological testing and imaging results are consistent with <u>active TB</u> [[7]](/library/thXXfB)[[8]](/library/ydcdsY0)

* Treatment

* Combination of <u>antibiotics</u>, most commonly given for 6 months  [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)

* Occasionally, invasive procedures (e.g., drainage for <u>pleural TB</u>) or <u>surgery</u> (e.g., <u>lobectomy</u> for <u>drug-resistant TB</u>) may be necessary. [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)[[10]](/library/jec_AY0)

* Drug-resistant tuberculosis [[11]](/library/r9bfKD)

* Definition: a form of TB that is resistant to one or more antitubercular agents

* Types

* <u>Rifampin</u>-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB): resistance to <u>rifampin</u> with or without resistance to other antitubercular drugs

* Monoresistant TB: resistance to one of the first-line antitubercular drugs

* <u>Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis</u> (<u>MDR-TB</u>): resistance to both <u>isoniazid</u> and <u>rifampin</u>

* Pre-extensively <u>drug-resistant TB</u> (<u>Pre-XDR-TB</u>): resistance to <u>isoniazid</u>, <u>rifampin</u>, and either any <u>fluoroquinolone</u> or a second-line injectable agent (e.g., <u>amikacin</u>, <u>kanamycin</u>, or <u>capreomycin</u>) [[12]](/library/OxWI9n0)

* <u>Extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis</u> (<u>XDR-TB</u>): resistance to <u>isoniazid</u>, <u>rifampin</u>, any <u>fluoroquinolone</u>, and either one of the second-line injectable drugs (e.g., <u>amikacin</u>, <u>kanamycin</u>, or <u>capreomycin</u>) or bedaquiline or <u>linezolid</u> [[12]](/library/OxWI9n0)

* Causes

* Incorrect drug combination therapy

* Inadequate duration or dosage of drug therapy

* Poor <u>treatment adherence</u>

* Poor quality of drugs

* Close contact with an individual with <u>drug-resistant TB</u>

## Epidemiology

* United States [[13]](/library/jwb_iD)

* The <u>incidence</u> of TB infection in the US has been slowly declining.

* The <u>incidence rate</u> for 2018 was 2.8 cases per 100,000 population.

* Two-thirds of new TB cases reported in the US in 2019 were in individuals born outside the US.

* The <u>prevalence</u> of <u>LTBI</u> in the United States is estimated to be 5% [[14]](/library/YDYn1r)

* Worldwide [[15]](/library/XDb91D)

* A leading <u>cause of death</u> from a single infectious agent

* The overall <u>incidence</u> and <u>prevalence</u> have been declining.

* The <u>incidence rate</u> for 2018 was 132 cases per 100,000 population.

* One-fourth of the world's population has <u>latent TB</u>.

* The sex <u>ratio</u> varies across countries and communities and largely depends on social and <u>cultural factors</u>.  [[16]](/library/QwbuiD)

* Countries with the highest <u>incidence</u> of TB: India, Indonesia, China, the Philippines, Bangladesh, Nigeria, Pakistan, and South Africa

* The <u>incidence</u> of multidrug-resistant TB is steadily rising.





![Tuberculosis fact sheet and incidence map](media/c9vuujnptuhpfk2e35gb0207.jpg)

Tuberculosis fact sheet and incidence map




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

## Etiology

### <u>Mycobacteria</u>




#### Species




<u>Mycobacterium</u> species that cause tuberculosis are collectively known as the <u>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</u> complex, which includes:




* <u>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</u> 

* Mode of transmission: spread via aerosol <u>droplet nuclei</u>

* Reservoir: predominantly humans

* Disease: all forms of tuberculosis

* Mycobacterium bovis

* Mode of transmission: predominantly via ingestion of contaminated cow's milk

* Reservoir: predominantly cattle

* Disease: <u>gastrointestinal tuberculosis</u> in humans

* <u>Mycobacterium</u> africanum: common cause of tuberculosis in West, Central, and East Africa [[1]](/library/kIYm1q)

* <u>Mycobacterium microti</u>





![Mycobacteria](media/cdsm67l1nug5b8heedx2ys4l.jpg)

Mycobacteria




#### Features of <u>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</u>




* Type: facultative intracellular rod-shaped bacteria

* <u>Gram stain</u>: does not stain well  [[17]](/library/S9by5D)[[18]](/library/R9blMD)

* Special stains

* <u>Ziehl-Neelsen stain</u>: <u>acid-fast bacilli</u> appear pink    [[19]](/library/g9bF5D)

* <u>Auramine-rhodamine stain</u> [[20]](/library/i9bJMD)

* <u>Acid-fast bacilli</u> appear reddish-yellow on fluorescence microscopy.

* Used as a screening tool because of high <u>sensitivity</u> and low cost

* Culture mediums for growth 

* <u>Löwenstein Jensen medium</u>

* <u>Middlebrook medium</u>

* Rapid automated broth culture

* Mechanism of resistance

* Remains viable in airborne <u>droplet nuclei</u> and soil  [[21]](/library/j9b_MD)

* Able to survive in acidic conditions [[22]](/library/P9bWnD)

* <u>Virulence factors</u>: See “Pathophysiology” below.





![Mycobacterium tuberculosis](media/vgg36gxbolpdv0fi52y624mn.jpg)

Mycobacterium tuberculosis

![Mycobacterium tuberculosis](media/rieh5z1alnsb88np2dg60ita.jpg)

Mycobacterium tuberculosis

![Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture](media/ss114ita3bu272bzoiksjcz5.jpg)

Mycobacterium tuberculosis culture




### Risk factors for tuberculosis exposure [[23]](/library/_5Y55p)




* Working in the health care industry

* Migration from countries with a high TB <u>incidence</u> (≥ 100 cases per 100,000 population) [[2]](/library/79b4KD)

* Frequent travel to <u>countries with a high TB burden</u>

* Close contact with a patient with <u>active TB infection</u>

* Crowded living conditions (e.g., prisons)

* Homelessness

## Pathophysiology

### <u>Primary tuberculosis</u> [[1]](/library/kIYm1q)[[3]](/library/p30Ljf)[[24]](/library/YxbnED)




#### <u>Innate immune response</u>




* Exposure to <u>M. tuberculosis</u>

* Individuals with <u>M. tuberculosis</u> infection disperse <u>droplet nuclei</u> that contain <u>bacilli</u> via sneezing or <u>coughing</u>.

* Inhaled <u>droplet nuclei</u> reach the terminal <u>alveoli</u> and are taken up by the <u>alveolar macrophages</u>.

* Entry into <u>macrophages</u>

* <u>Mycobacterial</u> <u>cell wall</u> contains <u>pathogen-associated molecular patterns</u> (<u>PAMPs</u>) such as <u>lipoarabinomannan</u> and lipomannan.

* <u>Alveolar macrophages</u> recognize <u>M. tuberculosis</u> <u>PAMPs</u> via <u>toll-like receptors</u> (TLRs)

* Activation of TLRs leads to the production of <u>proinflammatory cytokines</u> (e.g., <u>IL-1</u>, <u>IL-12</u>, <u>TNF-α</u>) and <u>phagocytosis</u> of <u>mycobacteria</u>.

* Replication within <u>macrophages</u>

* Typically, <u>phagocytosed</u> organisms reside within a <u>phagosome</u> to undergo intracellular killing via the following steps:

* <u>Phagosome</u> maturation: acidification using a proton pump system  [[25]](/library/cxbavD)

* Fusion of <u>phagosome</u> and <u>lysosome</u>: mediated by increased intracellular <u>calcium</u> levels [[26]](/library/1xb2vD)

* Killing of bacteria by <u>reactive oxygen species</u> (<u>ROS</u>), <u>reactive nitrogen intermediates</u> (<u>RNI</u>), and <u>lysosomal</u> enzymes

* <u>M. tuberculosis</u> survives within <u>macrophages</u> because of the inhibition of both <u>phagosome</u> maturation and <u>phagolysosome</u> fusion

* <u>Virulence factors</u> involved include: [[18]](/library/R9blMD)

* Cord factor (trehalose-6,6'-dimycolate): a surface <u>glycolipid</u> that causes serpentine cord-like growth, inhibits <u>neutrophil</u> migration, and induces <u>TNF-α</u> release to stimulate activated <u>macrophages</u> to form <u>granulomas</u>  [[27]](/library/VxbGvD)[[28]](/library/exbxvD)

* Sulfatides: surface <u>glycolipids</u> that inhibit <u>phagolysosome</u> fusion [[29]](/library/UxbbDD)

* Lipoarabinomannan: a lipoglycan that induces <u>TNF-α</u> release from <u>macrophages</u> and scavenges <u>ROS</u>

* <u>Catalase-peroxidase</u>: an enzyme that catalyzes the destruction of <u>ROS</u> and <u>H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub></u>

* <u>Macrophage</u> lysis and release of bacteria

* Following replication in the <u>alveolar macrophages</u>, the released bacteria attack uninfected <u>macrophages</u> to spread infection.

* <u>Dendritic cells</u> migrate to the site of infection and process <u>mycobacterial</u> <u>antigens</u>.

* Some bacteria enter the bloodstream, causing <u>bacteremia</u> and seeding multiple organs.





#### Cellular <u>immune response</u>




* <u>Th1 cell</u> activation

* <u>Dendritic cells</u> present <u>mycobacterial</u> <u>antigens</u> complexed with <u>MHC 2</u> to naive <u>T cells</u>

* Activated <u>CD4+ T cells</u> migrate to the focus of infection (<u>type IV HSR</u>).

* <u>Macrophage</u> activation and bacterial killing

* Activated <u>CD4+ T cells</u> release <u>IFN-γ</u>

* <u>IFN-γ</u> acts on <u>macrophages</u> to enable bacterial killing via the following mechanisms:

* Promotion of <u>phagosome</u> maturation

* Enhanced <u>RNI</u> production

* <u>Autophagy</u>

* <u>Granulomatous inflammation</u> and tissue destruction

* <u>IFN-γ</u>-activated <u>macrophages</u> secrete <u>TNF-α</u>.

* <u>TNF-α</u> promotes the aggregation of <u>macrophages</u> and <u>T cells</u> to form <u>granulomas</u>, affecting the <u>lungs</u> and regional <u>lymph nodes</u>

* Destruction of <u>M. tuberculosis</u>-infected <u>macrophages</u> causes central <u>caseous necrosis</u> and tissue damage.

* <u>Granuloma</u> limits the spread of infection.

* Ghon focus: a <u>granuloma</u> typically located in the middle/lower <u>lung</u> lobes.

* Ghon complex: formed by the <u>Ghon focus</u>, regional <u>lymph node</u>, and the linking lymphatic vessels

* Disease progression

* Sufficient <u>immune response</u>

* Most of the bacteria are killed.

* Some bacteria may persist, causing <u>LTBI</u>.

* The <u>granulomas</u> in the <u>Ghon complex</u> undergo <u>fibrosis</u> and calcification to form the Ranke complex.

* Deficient <u>immune response</u> (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>malnutrition</u>)

* Failure of <u>granulomas</u> to limit infection

* <u>Progressive primary TB</u> causing progressive <u>lung</u> disease, <u>bacteremia</u>, and <u>miliary TB</u>





![Tuberculous granuloma with Langhans cells](media/ccxnj8r0b4wsvn3q34g6fafz.jpg)

Tuberculous granuloma with Langhans cells

![Pulmonary tuberculosis](media/vuf32yexhofleat8j3src2e5.jpg)

Pulmonary tuberculosis

![Caseous necrosis in lung tissue](media/nx562xaeua6whyswemeq8ei5.jpg)

![Ranke complex in tuberculosis](media/c0xun0iugmw71p86lox1j64r.jpg)

### <u>Secondary tuberculosis</u> [[24]](/library/YxbnED)




* <u>Latent TB</u>: Dynamic equilibrium is maintained between the host <u>immune response</u> and <u>M. tuberculosis</u>.

* Reactivation of disease: due to weakening of <u>immune response</u> (e.g., resulting from <u>HIV</u>, <u>TNF-α inhibitor</u> therapy)

* Disease progression

* <u>Caseating granulomas</u> with central <u>necrosis</u> and <u>Langhans giant cells</u> are characteristic features.

* Usually affects the upper lobes of the <u>lungs</u> because of higher oxygen tension

* Can also affect other organs (due to seeding of organs in <u>primary tuberculosis</u>)

* Prior sensitization to <u>mycobacterial</u> <u>antigens</u> results in a stronger inflammatory response, causing extensive tissue destruction, cavitation, and scarring.





![Stages of pulmonary tuberculosis](media/i0e5tf7tc6h1j4kxoxr5cuh0.jpg)

Stages of pulmonary tuberculosis

## Clinical features

<u>Latent tuberculosis infection</u> does not typically manifest with symptoms. Patients with <u>primary TB</u> are commonly asymptomatic.




### Pulmonary tuberculosis [[1]](/library/kIYm1q)




* Systemic

* Low-grade <u>fever</u> with night sweats

* Weight loss (often severe), <u>anorexia</u>

* Decreased appetite

* <u>Malaise</u>, <u>weakness</u>

* Pulmonary  

* Non-productive <u>cough</u>

* Symptoms of progression: productive <u>cough</u> with <u>purulent</u> <u>sputum</u>, <u>hemoptysis</u>

* <u>Shortness of breath</u>

* <u>Pleuritic chest pain</u>  [[30]](/library/cSXaAx)

* <u>Clinical examination</u>: Findings are nonspecific.

* General: <u>pallor</u>, <u>clubbing</u> (advanced disease), generalized wasting

* Chest examination: Findings vary depending on the type and degree of pulmonary involvement.

* Consolidation: dullness on percussion, <u>crackles</u>, diminished breath sounds

* Cavitation: <u>hyperresonance</u> on percussion, <u>amphoric breath sounds</u>

* Bronchial obstruction: <u>rhonchi</u>

* <u>Pleural effusion</u> and/or <u>empyema</u>: dullness on percussion, diminished breath sounds

* Other possible findings: <u>erythema nodosum</u>, <u>phlyctenular conjunctivitis</u>





> [!TIP]
> Depending on the degree of <u>immunosuppression</u>, TB in <u>HIV</u>-positive individuals may progress atypically or more rapidly.




> [!TIP]
> Always consider TB as a differential diagnosis in a young individual with <u>hemoptysis</u> and if treatment for other pulmonary conditions (e.g., <u>pneumonia</u>) does not improve symptoms.




### <u>Extrapulmonary tuberculosis</u>




See “<u>Extrapulmonary tuberculosis</u>” for respective clinical features.

## Diagnosis

This section reviews the diagnosis of <u>active tuberculosis infection</u>. For screening and diagnosis of <u>latent TB</u>, see the section “<u>Latent tuberculosis</u>.”




### Approach [[7]](/library/thXXfB)




* Initial workup in all patients

* Focused <u>patient history</u> (e.g., exposure to individuals with TB, history of visiting or living in <u>countries with a high TB burden</u>)

* Microbiological studies  

* Initial tests: microscopy examination for <u>acid-fast bacilli</u> (AFB), <u>nucleic acid amplification test</u> (<u>NAAT</u>)

* <u>Confirmatory test</u>: <u>mycobacterial</u> culture (<u>gold standard</u>)

* Drug susceptibility testing: indicated in certain circumstances to identify resistant <u>mycobacteria</u>

* Consider CT chest or <u>CXR</u>

* Suspicion for <u>extrapulmonary TB</u>: Additional invasive procedures (e.g., <u>lymph node</u> <u>biopsy</u>, <u>thoracocentesis</u>) may be required for bacteriological confirmation (see “<u>Extrapulmonary TB</u>”). [[31]](/library/q9bCoD)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Lung cancer</u> is an important differential diagnosis of pulmonary TB. Start investigations for <u>malignancy</u> in any patient with systemic symptoms (e.g., weight loss, persistent <u>fevers</u>, <u>anorexia</u>) and abnormal imaging.




> [!TIP]
> <u>PPD TST</u> and <u>IGRA</u> are <u>screening tests for latent TB</u> and do not aid in the diagnostics of <u>active TB</u>. [[7]](/library/thXXfB)




### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[1]](/library/kIYm1q)




Laboratory findings are mostly unspecific but can provide important information during initial <u>diagnostic stages</u>. Possible findings include:




* <u>CBC</u>: mild <u>leukocytosis</u> (common) , <u>anemia</u> (in advanced disease)

* <u>BMP</u>: mild <u>hyponatremia</u>

* <u>Liver chemistries</u>: ↑ in concomitant <u>liver</u> disease; useful as a baseline prior to treatment [[32]](/library/gicFIX0)

* Other nonspecific findings: ↑ <u>ESR</u>, <u>pyuria</u> in renal disease [[32]](/library/gicFIX0)





### Microbiological studies [[7]](/library/thXXfB)




Confirmation of the presence of tuberculosis <u>bacilli</u> in different samples is done by direct visualization, positive culture, or by detecting genetic material. Samples used for testing include: [[7]](/library/thXXfB)




* <u>Sputum</u> samples (most common): Obtain ≥ 3 samples separated by 8 to 24-hour intervals (should include at least one early morning sample).  [[7]](/library/thXXfB)[[33]](/library/UecbyY0)[[34]](/library/udcp7Y0)

* <u>Induced sputum</u>   [[34]](/library/udcp7Y0)

* <u>Gastric lavage</u>  [[35]](/library/9dcNHY0)

* <u>Bronchoalveolar lavage</u>

* <u>Extrapulmonary TB</u> suspected: Fluid specimens or tissue samples should be sent for cell count, chemistries, <u>AFB smear microscopy</u>, and <u>NAAT</u>.  [[7]](/library/thXXfB)





> [!WARNING]
> Because <u>sputum</u> induction carries a high risk of transmission to health care workers, the procedure must be performed under strict <u>infection control</u> precautions. [[36]](/library/_dc5sY0)




| <br>Microbiological tests for active TB [[7]](/library/thXXfB)[[37]](/library/fVckFY0)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test | Description | Advantages | Disadvantages |
| Acid-fast bacilli smear microscopy | <br>* <u>Ziehl Neelsen stain</u> or <u>auramine rhodamine stain</u> are used.<br><br> | <br><br>* Rapid detection<br><br>* Inexpensive<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Low <u>sensitivity</u>  [[37]](/library/fVckFY0)<br><br>* Cannot differentiate <u>M. tuberculosis</u> from other <u>nontuberculous mycobacteria</u>  [[38]](/library/TVc6FY0)<br><br>* Both viable and nonviable <u>mycobacteria</u> will stain.  [[39]](/library/LVcwEY0)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Nucleic acid amplification test</u> | <br><br>* For initial testing (along with <u>AFB smear microscopy</u> and culture) if clinical suspicion is high<br><br>* Used for confirmation of AFB positive smears [[7]](/library/thXXfB)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* High <u>specificity</u> and <u>sensitivity</u> (lower <u>sensitivity</u> in individuals with a negative AFB smear)  [[37]](/library/fVckFY0)<br><br>* Rapid diagnosis<br><br>* Rapid detection of drug-resistant strains  [[37]](/library/fVckFY0)<br><br>* Low cross-reactivity with <u>nontuberculous mycobacteria</u> [[37]](/library/fVckFY0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Requires laboratory equipment and trained staff, which may make use in resource-limited settings more difficult<br><br>* Both viable and nonviable <u>mycobacteria</u> are detectable. [[36]](/library/_dc5sY0)<br><br><br> |
| Culture | <br><br>* <u>Gold standard diagnostic test</u><br><br>* Provides information on drug susceptibility<br><br><br> | <br><br>* High <u>sensitivity</u>  [[37]](/library/fVckFY0)<br><br>* Species identification<br><br>* Identification of drug resistance<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Takes 2 to 6 weeks for positive cultures to develop  [[37]](/library/fVckFY0)<br><br>* Delays the initiation of treatment, especially <u>drug-resistant TB</u><br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Request AFB and cultures of every sample obtained; request <u>NAAT</u> for the initial respiratory sample along with microscopy and culture if clinical suspicion is high. [[7]](/library/thXXfB)




#### Drug susceptibility testing [[7]](/library/thXXfB)




* Standard culture: used to assess for drug susceptibility in most patients; results are available after several weeks.

* Rapid molecular testing : for select patients at high risk of resistant tuberculosis [[7]](/library/thXXfB)

* History of previously treated tuberculosis

* Contact with individuals with <u>MDR-TB</u>

* <u>HIV infection</u>

* Patients born or having lived for ≥ 1 year in a country with moderate to high TB <u>incidence</u> or high <u>MDR-TB</u> <u>prevalence</u>  [[7]](/library/thXXfB)





> [!TIP]
> A negative <u>AFB smear microscopy</u> result does not rule out pulmonary TB and a confirmatory culture should be obtained. [[7]](/library/thXXfB)




### Imaging [[7]](/library/thXXfB)[[8]](/library/ydcdsY0)[[40]](/library/FhXgfB)




* Indications: often performed as part of the diagnostic workup of patients with respiratory symptoms

* Modalities: <u>x-ray</u> or CT chest

* Findings

* Highly variable and nonspecific, but can help narrow the differential diagnosis

* In <u>primary TB</u>, <u>chest x-ray</u> is often normal.





| <br>Chest imaging findings in active TB [[32]](/library/gicFIX0)[[40]](/library/FhXgfB)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <u>Primary TB</u> (middle/lower lobes) | Postprimary (reactivation) TB |
| <br><u>Chest x-ray</u>  <br> | <br><br>* Consolidation (homogeneous with ill-defined borders)<br><br>* Hilar <u>lymphadenopathy</u> (commonly unilateral)<br><br>* <u>Ghon complex</u><br><br>* <u>Pleural effusion</u><br><br>* Cavitation (rare)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Consolidation (patchy or confluent)<br><br>* Fibrocaseous cavitary lesions in upper lobes<br><br>* Calcifications<br><br><br> |
| <br>CT chest  <br> | <br>* <u>Enlarged lymph nodes</u> with low-attenuation center indicating central <u>necrosis</u> [[8]](/library/ydcdsY0)<br><br> | <br><br>* Thick-walled cavities without an <u>air-fluid level</u><br><br>* <u>Tree-in-bud pattern</u><br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Extensive cavitation can lead to areas of <u>bronchiectasis</u> and damaged <u>lung</u> areas can be colonized with <u>Aspergillus</u> spp., leading to <u>aspergillomas</u>, sometimes referred to as fungus balls. [[32]](/library/gicFIX0)




> [!WARNING]
> Normal imaging does not rule out TB. Although radiographic changes are common in immunocompetent patients, individuals who are <u>immunocompromised</u> can have normal imaging findings. [[8]](/library/ydcdsY0)[[31]](/library/q9bCoD)[[40]](/library/FhXgfB)

### <u>HIV</u> and TB <u>coinfection</u>




Diagnosing TB in patients with <u>HIV</u> <u>coinfection</u> is challenging because these individuals often have a negative AFB smear and commonly have atypical imaging findings resulting from paucibacillary disease due to a reduced <u>immune response</u>. Different measures can be used to increase diagnostic <u>sensitivity</u>. [[31]](/library/q9bCoD)[[36]](/library/_dc5sY0)




* Advanced testing in patients with <u>HIV</u> (not widely available) [[36]](/library/_dc5sY0)

* For most patients: fluorescent <u>AFB smear microscopy</u> , specialized culture mediums

* For patients with severe disease and those with a <u>CD4 count</u> < 100/mmÂ³: <u>lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan assay</u> [[41]](/library/WiXPqB)[[42]](/library/n1c7hY0)[[43]](/library/2VcTFY0)

* In resource-limited settings: a lower threshold for defining smear positivity and consideration of empiric treatment may be necessary  [[36]](/library/_dc5sY0)





> [!TIP]
> In patients with <u>HIV</u>, the <u>sensitivity</u> of routine initial microbiological studies may be low; additional investigations may be required.




> [!TIP]
> Obtain <u>HIV tests</u> in all patients with suspected (rather than confirmed) TB, as this can help to interpret test results. [[36]](/library/_dc5sY0)

## Differential diagnoses

### Pulmonary TB




* <u>Typical pneumonia</u>

* <u>Atypical pneumonia</u>

* <u>COVID-19</u> <u>pneumonia</u>

* <u>Lung cancer</u>

* <u>Lung abscess</u>

* <u>Interstitial lung disease</u>

* See “<u>Differential diagnosis of granulomatous disease</u>.”

* <u>Sarcoidosis</u>

* <u>Hodgkin lymphoma</u>

* <u>Non-Hodgkin lymphoma</u>

* <u>Pneumoconiosis</u>

* <u>Granulomatosis with polyangiitis</u>

* <u>Histoplasmosis</u>

* See “Nontuberculous <u>mycobacterial</u> infections” and “<u>Mycobacterium avium complex infection</u>.”

* <u>Brucellosis</u>

* <u>Tularemia</u>





### <u>Extrapulmonary TB</u>




* <u>Leprosy</u>

* <u>Syphilis</u>

* <u>Erythema nodosum</u>

* <u>Lymphoma</u>

* <u>Multiple myeloma</u>

* <u>Rheumatoid arthritis</u>

* <u>Systemic lupus erythematosus</u>





The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

## Treatment

This section reviews the <u>treatment of active tuberculosis</u>. For the treatment of <u>latent TB</u>, see the section “<u>Latent tuberculosis</u>.”




### General principles [[1]](/library/kIYm1q)[[9]](/library/L3XwQB)




* Goals 

* Reduction of disease severity and risk of transmission

* Eradication of all <u>bacilli</u> to achieve sustained cure without relapse following completion of treatment

* Prevention of drug resistance during therapy

* <u>Infection control</u> measures 

* Case notification: mandatory reporting to local health department  [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)

* <u>Airborne precautions</u>: should include a <u>surgical mask</u> for the patient and adequate <u>personal protective equipment</u> (including <u>respirators</u>) for medical staff and caregivers  [[45]](/library/n3X7QB)

* <u>Contact tracing</u>: See “Prevention” section for testing indications.

* <u>Antituberculosis therapy</u>

* All patients should undergo a pretreatment evaluation.

* Choice of pharmacologic therapy is based on the site of infection and drug susceptibility.





### Indications for treatment [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)




* Confirmed <u>active TB</u>

* Positive culture for <u>M. tuberculosis</u>

* Positive <u>NAAT</u> (with positive or negative <u>AFB smear microscopy</u>)

* Suspected <u>active TB</u>: Consider empiric treatment in all patients pending test results.

* Factors favoring empiric treatment: high risk of disease progression and/or dissemination , imaging consistent with <u>active TB</u>, positive screening , critically ill patients, high transmission risk

* Factors favoring delayed therapy: no known TB exposure, high risk of therapy side effects, negative <u>NAAT</u> (with positive or negative <u>AFB smear microscopy</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Empiric treatment with standard <u>antituberculosis therapy</u> is indicated in most cases in which active infection is suspected. [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)




### Pretreatment evaluation [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)




* Clinical assessment 

* Weight

* Nutritional assessment

* Symptom review

* <u>Eye exam</u>: <u>visual acuity</u> and color discrimination

* Microbiology: <u>sputum</u> smear microscopy and culture, drug susceptibility testing

* Imaging: <u>chest x-ray</u> or other chest imaging

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* All patients: <u>liver chemistries</u>; , <u>platelet count</u>, <u>BMP</u>, <u>HIV screening</u>

* Depending on risk: <u>hepatitis B</u> and <u>hepatitis C</u> screening, <u>diabetes</u> screen, β-<u>HCG</u> in individuals who can become pregnant





### Antituberculosis therapy




Consultation with infectious disease experts is advised.




#### RIPE TB regimen [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)[[46]](/library/lxWv9n0)




* Intensive phase: : 8 weeks (∼ 2 months) of <u>rifampin</u>  DOSAGE PLUS <u>isoniazid</u> DOSAGE, <u>pyrazinamide</u> DOSAGE , and <u>ethambutol</u> DOSAGE  [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)

* Continuation phase: : 18 weeks (∼ 4 months) of <u>rifampin</u>  DOSAGE PLUS <u>isoniazid</u> DOSAGE  [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)

* <u>Adjuvant treatment</u>: : <u>pyridoxine</u>  DOSAGE to prevent <u>vitamin B<sub>6</sub> deficiency</u> resulting from <u>isoniazid</u> (promotes <u>pyridoxine</u> excretion) for all individuals at risk of neuropathy  [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)

* Additional considerations

* Self-administered and daily dosages are preferred

* Directly observed therapy (DOT; standard practice): <u>Health care personnel</u> observe the patient taking the medication.

* Restart full treatment if there is an interruption of ≥ 14 days during the intensive phase.





> [!TIP]
> <u>RIPE TB regimen</u> consists of 6 months of <u>rifampin</u> and <u>isoniazid</u> plus <u>pyrazinamide</u> and <u>ethambutol</u> during the first 2 months.




> [!NOTE]
> "<u>RIPE</u>": Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol




> [!TIP]
> The long duration of treatment for <u>active TB</u> requires <u>patient-centered</u> coordination with primary care and specialist services and <u>directly observed therapy</u> (DOT) to ensure adherence. [[47]](/library/P3XWiB)




#### 4-month regimen for TB [[46]](/library/lxWv9n0)[[48]](/library/NxW-9n0)[[49]](/library/wqdh0r0)




This regimen may be considered for patients with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB who are age ≥ 12 years, ≥ 40 kg, and without contraindications (e.g., drug-<u>drug interactions</u>, <u>prolonged QT</u> syndrome, <u>pregnancy</u>).




* Intensive phase: 8 weeks of <u>rifapentine</u> DOSAGE, <u>isoniazid</u> DOSAGE, <u>pyrazinamide</u> DOSAGE, and <u>moxifloxacin</u> DOSAGE

* Continuation phase: 9 weeks of <u>rifapentine</u> DOSAGE, <u>isoniazid</u> DOSAGE, and <u>moxifloxacin</u> DOSAGE

* <u>Adjuvant treatment</u>: <u>Pyridoxine</u> DOSAGE to prevent <u>vitamin B<sub>6</sub> deficiency</u> resulting from <u>isoniazid</u>

* Additional considerations: DOT should be implemented during the treatment period.





#### Treatment of <u>drug-resistant TB</u> disease [[10]](/library/jec_AY0)[[49]](/library/wqdh0r0)




This includes <u>MDR-TB</u> and <u>XDR-TB</u>. Consultation with infectious disease experts is required.




* Agents

* Oral: later-generation <u>fluoroquinolone</u> (e.g., <u>moxifloxacin</u>), bedaquiline, <u>linezolid</u>, <u>clofazimine</u>, <u>cycloserine</u>, pretomanid [[50]](/library/jxW_wn0)

* IV: <u>amikacin</u>, <u>streptomycin</u>, and <u>carbapenem</u> with <u>amoxicillin-clavulanic acid</u>

* Phases of treatment: combine at least 3–5 agents for the intensive and continuation phases

* Role of <u>surgery</u>: Elective partial <u>lung</u> <u>surgery</u> can be beneficial.





> [!TIP]
> An all-oral regimen (i.e., bedaquilline, pretomanid, and <u>linezolid</u> ± <u>moxifloxacin</u>) may be considered for <u>drug-resistant TB</u> based on drug susceptibility. [[49]](/library/wqdh0r0)




#### Treatment of extrapulmonary TB [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)




Choose antimicrobials under specialist guidance and tailor choice and duration of therapy to the infection site, severity, and response.




* Standard <u>antituberculosis therapy</u> (e.g., 6-month <u>RIPE TB regimen</u>): used for <u>lymph node</u>, pleural, miliary, <u>pericardial</u>, <u>adrenal</u>, gastrointestinal, and <u>genitourinary TB</u>

* Extended regimens

* <u>TB meningoencephalitis</u> (9–12 months of therapy)

* 2 months of 4-drug intensive phase, followed by 7–10 months of continuation phase with <u>isoniazid</u> and <u>rifampin</u>

* See <u>RIPE TB regimen</u> for daily dosages.

* Adjunctive <u>glucocorticoid</u> treatment with <u>dexamethasone</u> or <u>prednisolone</u> for 6–8 weeks

* <u>Pott disease</u> and other bone and <u>joint</u> TB

* Typically 6–9 months of therapy

* May be extended up to 12 months

* <u>Surgery</u> in select patients





> [!TIP]
> Consultation with a specialist is always advised in all patients with <u>extrapulmonary TB</u>, especially for miliary disease.




### Side effects of antituberculosis agents [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)




Mild side effects can usually be managed with symptomatic treatment, while more severe side effects (e.g., significant <u>hepatotoxicity</u>, <u>optic neuritis</u>) usually require one or more drugs to be discontinued and replaced in consultation with a specialist.



* General side effects: may be caused by any of the drugs commonly used in standard <u>antituberculosis therapy</u>

* <u>Hepatotoxicity</u> (most common serious side effect)

* <u>Rash</u>, <u>pruritus</u>

* GI symptoms

* Allergic and <u>nonallergic hypersensitivity</u> reactions




| <br>Specific side effects of antituberculosis drugs [[9]](/library/L3XwQB) |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Isoniazid</u> | <br><br>* Asymptomatic elevation of <u>transaminases</u><br><br>* <u>Cytochrome P450 inhibition</u>: leading to interactions with numerous drugs, including antiretroviral agents, cardiovascular agents, and <u>antibiotics</u><br><br>* Less common<br><br>* <u>Drug-induced lupus</u><br><br>* <u>Vitamin B<sub>6</sub> deficiency</u>: <u>sideroblastic anemia</u>, <u>peripheral neuropathy</u>  [[51]](/library/gecFyY0)<br><br>* <u>CNS</u> toxicity: precipitation of <u>benzodiazepine</u>-refractory <u>seizures</u> with high doses of <u>isoniazid</u>, <u>psychosis</u>, <u>ataxia</u> [[52]](/library/ReclAY0)[[53]](/library/SecyyY0)[[54]](/library/heccAY0)<br><br>* Others: <u>anion gap metabolic acidosis</u>, <u>pellagra</u>, <u>optic neuritis</u> [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)[[52]](/library/ReclAY0)[[55]](/library/iecJAY0)<br><br><br> |
| <u>Rifampin</u> | <br><br>* Transient asymptomatic elevation of <u>bilirubin</u>, clinical <u>hepatitis</u> with a <u>cholestatic injury pattern</u><br><br>* <u>Cytochrome P450 induction</u>: leading to important interactions with <u>ART</u> in patients with <u>HIV</u> (therefore, <u>rifabutin</u> is preferred)<br><br>* Orange discoloration of body fluids (e.g., urine, tears)<br><br>* <u>Thrombocytopenia</u><br><br>* <u>False-positive</u> result on urine <u>opiate</u> screening<br><br><br> |
| <u>Pyrazinamide</u> | <br><br>* Greatest <u>hepatotoxicity</u> potential<br><br>* <u>Hyperuricemia</u>  [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)<br><br>* <u>Arthralgia</u><br><br>* <u>Photosensitivity</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Ethambutol</u> | <br><br>* <u>Optic neuritis</u> (reversible red-green <u>color blindness</u>)<br><br>* <u>Hyperuricemia</u> [[56]](/library/63XjjB)<br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Rifampin</u> and <u>isoniazid</u> alter the <u>efficacy</u> of drugs metabolized by <u>cytochrome P450</u> (especially <u>protease inhibitors</u>, <u>NNRTIs</u>, <u>OCPs</u>, <u>warfarin</u>, <u>sulfonylureas</u>).




![Orange urine secondary to rifampicin therapy](media/t1nhtff3saxqvcibgpgagbif.jpg)

Orange urine secondary to rifampicin therapy




### Monitoring [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)[[44]](/library/V3XGhB)




Monthly follow-ups are recommended in all patients receiving antituberculosis treatment for <u>active TB</u> or <u>LTBI</u>.




* All patients

* Assess adherence to therapy.

* Perform a symptom review and screen for <u>clinical features of active TB</u>.

* Monitor for side effects.

* Patients with <u>active TB</u>

* <u>Sputum</u> smear microscopy and culture

* Weight and <u>vision</u> assessment

* <u>Laboratory studies</u>: If indicated, obtain <u>liver chemistries</u>, <u>platelet count</u>, and <u>creatinine</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Advise patients to self-monitor for features that suggest <u>hepatitis</u> (e.g., <u>jaundice</u>, fatigue, <u>anorexia</u>, abdominal <u>pain</u>) and seek prompt medical attention if any of them arise. [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)

---

## Latent tuberculosis infection

### Description




* A state of constant <u>immune response</u> stimulation due to <u>M. tuberculosis</u> <u>antigens</u>, with no signs of <u>active TB infection</u>

* Individuals with <u>latent TB</u> are asymptomatic and not contagious.





> [!TIP]
> <u>M. tuberculosis</u> remains dormant within the host and may be reactivated once the <u>immune system</u> becomes compromised (e.g., by high doses of <u>glucocorticoids</u> or <u>chemotherapeutic agents</u>, <u>HIV infection</u>).




### <u>Epidemiology</u> [[14]](/library/YDYn1r)




* The <u>prevalence</u> of <u>LTBI</u> in the United States is estimated to be 5%.

* 5–10% of untreated cases progress to <u>active TB</u> if left untreated.





### Diagnosis [[7]](/library/thXXfB)[[44]](/library/V3XGhB)




#### Screening for LTBI  [[7]](/library/thXXfB)[[57]](/library/ESW8YO0)[[58]](/library/mc1V1f0)




The decision of whether to test an individual should be carefully considered based on the likelihood of someone having <u>LTBI</u>, the likelihood of progression of <u>LTBI</u> to <u>active TB</u>, and the potential benefit of therapy.




* Individuals with a high likelihood of <u>LTBI</u> (i.e., high risk of TB exposure; see also “<u>Risk factors for tuberculosis</u>”) [[7]](/library/thXXfB)[[44]](/library/V3XGhB)

* Known contact with AFB smear-positive individual

* Individuals born in or former residents of <u>countries with a high TB burden</u> (> 20 cases per 100,000 population)  [[58]](/library/mc1V1f0)

* People who live or work in high-risk settings (e.g., correctional facilities, long-term care facilities or <u>nursing homes</u>, homeless shelters)

* Health-care workers who care for patients at increased risk for <u>TB disease</u>

* Children (< 18 years of age) exposed to adults at increased risk for tuberculosis infection

* Individuals with a high likelihood of progression from <u>LTBI</u> to <u>active TB</u> [[7]](/library/thXXfB)[[44]](/library/V3XGhB)

* High <u>risk factors</u>:

* <u>HIV infection</u>

* <u>Immunosuppressive therapy</u>, including: [[59]](/library/tVcXwY0)

* <u>Corticosteroid</u> therapy  [[60]](/library/cwba3D)[[61]](/library/1wb23D)

* <u>TNF-α inhibitor</u> therapy (e.g., <u>infliximab</u>)  [[62]](/library/WwbP3D)

* Others: <u>methotrexate</u>, <u>cyclosporine</u>; drugs used for organ transplant and <u>stem cell</u> transplant recipients

* <u>Silicosis</u>

* Age < 5 years

* Prior TB infection

* Intermediate <u>risk factors</u>: <u>diabetes</u>, <u>chronic kidney disease</u>, IV drug use

* Other <u>risk factors</u>:

* Smoking  [[63]](/library/VwbG3D)

* <u>Heavy alcohol consumption</u>  [[64]](/library/UwbbRD)

* <u>Malnutrition</u>, low <u>body mass index</u>

* Advanced age  [[65]](/library/dwbo3D)

* <u>Malignancy</u>

* <u>Gastrectomy</u> or jejunoileal bypass





> [!TIP]
> All patients with <u>HIV</u> should be screened for <u>LTBI</u>, regardless of additional <u>risk factors</u>. [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)




> [!TIP]
> All individuals due to start <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u> should be screened for <u>LTBI</u>. [[59]](/library/tVcXwY0)




#### Selection of <u>screening test</u> [[7]](/library/thXXfB)




* Most patients: <u>IGRA</u> (preferred in those who have had the <u>BCG</u> <u>vaccine</u>) or <u>PPD TST</u>  [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)

* Patients with <u>HIV</u>, children aged < 5 years, <u>immunocompromised</u> patients

* <u>PPD TST</u> and <u>chest x-ray</u>

* OR <u>IGRA</u> and <u>chest x-ray</u>





| <br>Screening tests for LTBI [[7]](/library/thXXfB)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | <br>Purified protein derivative tuberculin skin test (<u>Mantoux test</u>) [[66]](/library/yVcdCY0)<br> | <br>Interferon-γ release assay (<u>IGRA</u>) [[67]](/library/CVcq9Y0)<br> |
| Mechanism | <br>* Tests <u>cell-mediated immunity</u> against <u>M. tuberculosis</u> via <u>delayed hypersensitivity reaction</u> (<u>type IV HSR</u>) mounted by <u>T cells</u><br><br> | <br>* Tests <u>cell-mediated immunity</u> against <u>M. tuberculosis</u>-specific <u>antigens</u> by measuring the amount of <u>IFN-γ</u> released by <u>T cells</u> using <u>ELISA</u><br><br> |
| Procedure | <br><br>* <u>Step 1</u>: 0.1 mL (or 5 units) of purified protein derivative (<u>PPD</u>) injected intradermally on the <u>volar</u> surface of the forearm resulting in <u>wheal</u> formation<br><br>* <u>Step 2</u>: transverse diameter of palpable induration checked 48–72 hours later<br><br><br> | <br><br>* QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube (QFT) assay: Whole blood is drawn into three test tubes in the following order: [[68]](/library/AVcRCY0)<br>1. * Negative control tube<br>2. * TB <u>antigen</u> test tube<br>3. * Positive control tube containing mitogen<br><br>* <u>T-SPOT.TB assay</u>: One sample of whole blood is required. [[67]](/library/CVcq9Y0)<br><br><br> |
| Benefits | <br><br>* Inexpensive<br><br>* Preferred test in children < 5 years of age [[7]](/library/thXXfB)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Only requires a single office visit<br><br>* Preferred test in individuals with prior <u>BCG</u> <u>vaccination</u><br><br>* Results are available within 24 hours. [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br><br><br> |
| Limitations | <br><br>* Does not differentiate between active and <u>latent TB</u><br><br>* Variability in test interpretation [[67]](/library/CVcq9Y0)<br><br>* Requires two office visits<br><br>* <u>False positives</u> resulting from either of the following:<br><br>* Prior <u>BCG</u> <u>vaccination</u>  [[69]](/library/1Nd2Zq0)<br><br>* Exposure to <u>nontuberculous mycobacteria</u><br><br>* <u>False negatives</u> are possible in patients with any of the following:<br><br>* <u>Sarcoidosis</u> [[70]](/library/S3cy3X0)<br><br>* <u>Immunosuppressed state</u> (<u>anergy</u>)<br><br>* Age < 6 months<br><br>* Recent (within 8–10 weeks) or very old (many years) TB infection<br><br>* Recent live-<u>virus</u> <u>vaccination</u><br><br>* <u>Disseminated TB</u> disease<br><br><br> | <br><br>* No differentiation between active and <u>latent TB</u><br><br>* Expensive [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br><br>* Errors in collecting and transporting blood can decrease <u>accuracy</u>.  [[14]](/library/YDYn1r)<br><br><br> |





![Positive Mantoux test](media/ypuq5wan9t19uu7m9tc88uxa.jpg)

Positive Mantoux test

![Tuberculin skin test (Mendel-Mantoux test)](media/trt89vj5fjjwe4q7yqhpnprp.jpg)

Tuberculin skin test (Mendel-Mantoux test)




#### Interpretation of results [[7]](/library/thXXfB)[[44]](/library/V3XGhB)




* <u>IGRA</u>

* Positive: TB infection is likely

* Negative: TB infection is unlikely, but cannot be excluded

* Indeterminate: can occur in inflammation or infection;   and/or <u>immunosuppressed</u> states (e.g., due to immunomodulatory medications and/or <u>HIV infection</u>), and a repeat <u>IGRA</u> or <u>PPD TST</u> can be useful [[71]](/library/0ecexY0)

* <u>PPD TST</u>: Depending on patient characteristics, a <u>PPD TST</u> can be positive with an induration ≥ 5 mm, ≥ 10 mm, or ≥ 15 mm.

* For healthy individuals with no <u>risk factors</u>, an induration < 15 mm is considered negative for TB.

* For patients with <u>BCG</u> <u>vaccination</u> history, interpret a <u>positive PPD TST according to induration diameter</u> and relevant <u>risk factors</u>.  [[69]](/library/1Nd2Zq0)





| <br>Positive PPD TST according to induration diameter [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
| ≥ 5 mm | <br><br>* Individuals exposed to AFB smear-positive case<br><br>* Individuals with <u>HIV</u><br><br>* Individuals with clinical or radiographic evidence of active or prior TB<br><br>* Individuals with organ transplants or receiving <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u><br><br><br> |
| ≥ 10 mm | <br><br>* Individuals who have moved within the last 5 years from a <u>country with a high TB burden</u> (> 20 cases per 100,000 population) [[7]](/library/thXXfB)<br><br>* Individuals living or working in high-risk settings (e.g., homeless shelters, prisons)<br><br>* Individuals who inject drugs<br><br>* Mycobacteriology laboratory workers<br><br>* Individuals with illnesses such as <u>diabetes</u> and <u>CKD</u><br><br>* Children < 5 years of age<br><br>* Children who have had contact with adults in high-risk categories<br><br>* Individuals with low <u>BMI</u><br><br><br> |
| ≥ 15 mm | <br>* All otherwise healthy individuals with no known <u>risk factors</u> [[72]](/library/kDYmer)<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> The diagnosis of <u>LTBI</u> is based on a positive screening result in patients with a <u>medical history</u> and <u>physical examination</u> consistent with latent disease, once <u>active TB</u> has been excluded. [[14]](/library/YDYn1r)




> [!WARNING]
> If <u>screening for LTBI</u> is positive, it is still necessary to exclude <u>active TB</u> prior to starting treatment for <u>LTBI</u> because neither <u>screening test</u> can differentiate between active and <u>latent infection</u>. [[14]](/library/YDYn1r)




#### Further evaluation




| <br>Management of individuals screened for TB [[73]](/library/G3XBPB)<br> |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  |  | Initial management | Further management |
| Positive <u>IGRA</u> or <u>TST</u> |  |  | <br><br>* <u>Chest x-ray</u> to exclude <u>active TB</u><br><br>* Individuals with low risk: Diagnosis can be confirmed with dual testing using the same or a different testing method. [[74]](/library/iB1J0j0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Chest x-ray</u> is normal: Treat for <u>LTBI</u>.<br><br>* <u>Chest x-ray</u> is abnormal: Work up for <u>active TB</u>.<br><br><br> |
| <u>IGRA</u> or <u>TST</u> negative | If < 8–10 weeks since exposure |  | <br><br>* Immunocompetent individuals and children ≥ 5 years of age: no treatment; repeat <u>screening test</u> 8–10 weeks following exposure.<br><br>* <u>Immunocompromised individuals</u> and children < 5 years of age: Start treatment for <u>LTBI</u> until <u>TST</u> or <u>IGRA</u> is repeated 8–10 weeks following exposure.<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Repeat <u>screening test</u> is positive: <u>chest x-ray</u><br><br>* <u>Chest x-ray</u> is normal: Treat for <u>LTBI</u>.<br><br>* <u>Chest x-ray</u> is abnormal: Work up for <u>active TB</u>.<br><br>* Repeat <u>screening test</u> is negative<br><br>* No treatment is required; stop treatment if already initiated.<br><br>* <u>HIV</u> patients: Consider completing <u>LTBI</u> treatment if exposed to an individual with <u>active TB</u>.<br><br><br> |
| If > 8–10 weeks since exposure |  | <br>* No further evaluation is required.<br><br> |  |  |





> [!TIP]
> If health care workers are exposed to an individual with <u>active TB</u> without adequate <u>personal protective equipment</u>, <u>IGRA</u> or <u>PPD TST</u> must be performed immediately and repeated after 8–10 weeks if the initial test is negative. [[75]](/library/ViXGqB)




#### Special situations [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)




* <u>HIV infection</u>: Screen for <u>LTBI</u> at the time of diagnosis and repeat annually in patients at risk of exposure.

* <u>BCG</u> <u>vaccination</u>: <u>IGRA</u> is preferred to <u>PPD TST</u>.  [[69]](/library/1Nd2Zq0)

* Screening prior to starting <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>: Follow the usual screening algorithm, but consider a second test if the initial <u>screening test</u> is negative.  [[76]](/library/k4cmjc0)

* Individuals who are periodically tested with <u>PPD TST</u>

* <u>TST</u> results may be affected by <u>booster phenomenon</u>

* Consider two-step <u>TST</u> in select cases to avoid misinterpretation; two-step testing is not required if <u>IGRA</u> is used as a baseline test. 

* Method: initial baseline <u>TST</u> and a second <u>TST</u> 1–3 weeks later

* Interpretation: Repeat <u>TST</u> is considered positive if <u>TST</u> conversion occurs.  [[77]](/library/WecPBY0)

* Negative repeat <u>TST</u>: <u>LTBI</u> is unlikely and no further management is required.

* Positive repeat <u>TST</u>: A boosted reaction has occurred and <u>LTBI</u> is likely and requires further management.





### Treatment




> [!TIP]
> The primary goal of the treatment of <u>latent TB</u> is to prevent reactivation to <u>active TB</u>.




#### Pretreatment considerations [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)




* Medical and drug history

* Baseline <u>liver chemistries</u> (for all individuals at risk of <u>liver</u> injury)

* Exclusion of <u>active TB</u>: Patients should have no clinical or radiological evidence of TB. 

* Most patients: Obtain <u>AFB smear microscopy</u> ONLY if symptoms or radiological features are identified.

* Patients with <u>HIV</u>: Consider <u>AFB smear microscopy</u> regardless of symptoms or radiological features.

* Case notification: Reporting to the local health department is advised and may be mandatory in some locations.

* <u>Infection control</u>: <u>Airborne precautions</u> are not required once active pulmonary TB has been excluded. [[78]](/library/mecVzY0)

* Patient education: Provide information about treatment and its side effects, methods available to support adherence to therapy, and instructions to seek medical attention if side effects occur.





#### Pharmacotherapy of <u>LTBI</u> [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)




* Pharmacological therapy: indicated for patients with positive <u>IGRA</u> or <u>PPD TST</u> after <u>active TB</u> has been excluded

* <u>Rifamycin</u>-based short regimens are preferred.

* Long regimens may be considered based on <u>drug tolerance</u>, pharmacological interactions, and <u>HIV</u> status.





| <br>Drug regimens for treatment of LTBI [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Detailed regimen | Indications |
| Short regimens | <br><br>* Once-weekly <u>isoniazid</u> DOSAGEPLUS once-weekly <u>rifapentine</u> DOSAGE for 3 months (abbreviation: 3HP) [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br><br>* PLUS once-weekly <u>pyridoxine</u> DOSAGE (for all individuals at risk of <u>peripheral neuropathy</u> from <u>INH</u>)  [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Most patients > 2 years of age<br><br>* Select patients with <u>HIV</u>/<u>AIDS</u><br><br><br> |
| <br><br>* Once-daily <u>isoniazid</u> DOSAGE PLUS once-daily <u>rifampin</u> DOSAGE for 3 months (abbreviation: 3HR) [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br><br>* PLUS once-daily <u>pyridoxine</u> DOSAGE (for all individuals at risk of <u>peripheral neuropathy</u> from <u>INH</u>)  [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br><br><br> |  |  |
| <br>* Once-daily <u>rifampin</u> DOSAGE for 4 months (abbreviation: 4R) [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br><br> | <br>* <u>HIV</u>-negative patients of any age who:<br><br>* Are unable to tolerate <u>INH</u><br><br>* OR have been exposed to <u>INH</u>-resistant TB<br><br> |  |
| Long regimens | <br><br>* Once-daily <u>isoniazid</u> DOSAGE for 6 months (abbreviation: 6H)  [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br><br>* Once-daily <u>isoniazid</u> DOSAGE for 9 months (abbreviation: 9H)  [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br><br>* PLUS <u>pyridoxine</u> DOSAGE (for all individuals at risk of <u>peripheral neuropathy</u> from <u>INH</u>)  [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Most patients with <u>HIV</u><br><br>* Patients of any age with contraindications for <u>rifamycins</u> [[79]](/library/p3XLjB)<br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Rifampin</u> and <u>rifapentine</u> are not interchangeable and clinicians and pharmacists should be careful to prescribe and administer the correct drug.

---

## Extrapulmonary tuberculosis

This section provides an overview of the most common types of <u>extrapulmonary tuberculosis</u>.




### Tuberculous lymphadenitis [[80]](/library/MTXMrx)




* Pathophysiology

* Hematogenous dissemination following <u>primary TB</u>

* Local extension of infection from the affected organ

* Sites of <u>lymph node</u> involvement

* Cervical

* Inguinal

* Axillary

* Clinical features

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>

* <u>Lymphadenopathy</u>: Findings vary depending on the stage of <u>lymphadenitis</u>.  [[81]](/library/nTX7rx)

* <u>Lymphadenitis</u>: firm, mobile, and discrete <u>lymph nodes</u>

* Periadenitis: rubbery and fixed <u>lymph nodes</u>

* <u>Cold abscess</u>: soft and <u>fluctuant</u> <u>lymph nodes</u>

* <u>Draining sinus</u> tract

* Diagnostics [[80]](/library/MTXMrx)

* <u>Ultrasound</u> or CT: matted <u>lymph nodes</u> with a <u>necrotic</u> center

* <u>FNAC</u> or <u>excisional biopsy</u>

* <u>Acid-fast bacilli</u>

* <u>Granulomatous inflammation</u>

* Treatment: See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”





### Tuberculous hilar lymphadenopathy [[1]](/library/kIYm1q)[[82]](/library/23XT3B)




* Pathophysiology

* Lymphatic spread of <u>M. tuberculosis</u> from the <u>lung</u> during <u>primary TB</u> infection

* <u>Bronchus</u> compression

* Total: causes <u>distal airway</u> collapse

* Partial: causes ball-valve effect and hyperinflation

* Clinical features

* Commonly seen in children

* <u>Wheezing</u>

* Mostly asymptomatic

* Diagnostics: <u>chest x-ray</u> or CT

* Unilateral or bilateral enlarged <u>hilar lymph nodes</u>

* <u>Lung</u> <u>atelectasis</u>

* Hyperinflation

* Treatment: See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”





![Lymphadenopathy and miliary lung nodules](media/j727781qsce3usd5wzd8ed4t.jpg)

Lymphadenopathy and miliary lung nodules




### Tuberculous pleurisy [[83]](/library/5TXirx)




* Pathophysiology

* Direct spread of infection from the <u>lungs</u>

* Hematogenous spread

* <u>Delayed hypersensitivity reaction</u> in the <u>pleural space</u> due to <u>mycobacterial</u> <u>antigen</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>

* Nonproductive <u>cough</u>

* Intensive (pleuritic) <u>chest pain</u>

* <u>Dyspnea</u>

* Diagnostics

* Imaging

* <u>Chest x-ray</u>: unilateral <u>pleural effusion</u>

* Chest <u>ultrasound</u> or CT: <u>loculated</u> effusion with septations; pleural thickening

* <u>Thoracentesis</u>: <u>pleural fluid analysis</u> [[84]](/library/mTXVrx)

* <u>Exudative</u> type (<u>Light criteria</u>)

* <u>pH</u>: < 7.4

* <u>Glucose</u>: < 60 mg/dL

* ↑ <u>Adenosine deaminase</u>

* Rich in <u>lymphocytes</u>

* Microbiology: <u>acid-fast staining</u>, <u>PCR</u>, and culture

* <u>Sputum</u> smear examination: <u>acid-fast staining</u>

* Treatment 

* <u>Therapeutic thoracentesis</u> for symptom relief

* See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”





### Miliary tuberculosis [[85]](/library/ZTXZ6x)




* Definition: a form of TB with multiorgan involvement that manifests with granulomatous lesions (resembling millets) as a result of lymphohematogenous dissemination of <u>bacilli</u> from a pulmonary or extrapulmonary source

* <u>Epidemiology</u>: ∼ 20% of <u>extrapulmonary TB</u> cases [[86]](/library/weXhax)

* Pathophysiology: primary infection or reactivation

* Common sites of involvement: <u>lungs</u>, <u>spleen</u>, <u>liver</u>, <u>lymph nodes</u>, <u>adrenals</u>, <u>meninges</u>, <u>vertebrae</u> (<u>Pott disease</u>), <u>joints</u> and <u>long bones</u>, and <u>choroid</u>

* Clinical features: mostly nonspecific 

* <u>Cough</u> and <u>dyspnea</u>

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>

* <u>Lymphadenopathy</u>

* <u>Hepatosplenomegaly</u>

* Tuberculosis <u>miliaria</u> <u>cutis</u> disseminata

* Diagnostics: requires a high index of clinical suspicion

* <u>Fundoscopy</u>: <u>choroid</u> tubercles

* Microbiology: <u>sputum</u>, body fluids, and tissue 

* <u>Acid-fast staining</u>

* <u>PCR</u>

* Culture

* Blood

* ↑ <u>ESR</u> and <u>CRP</u>

* <u>CBC</u>: <u>anemia</u>, <u>leukopenia</u>

* <u>LFT</u>: <u>elevated transaminases</u> and <u>bilirubin</u>

* <u>Electrolytes</u>: <u>hyponatremia</u>, <u>hypercalcemia</u>

* <u>PPD TST</u>: negative

* Imaging

* <u>Chest x-ray</u>: multiple small <u>nodules</u> (< 2 mm) with an appearance resembling millet seeds  [[86]](/library/weXhax)

* <u>Ultrasound</u>: <u>pleural effusion</u>, <u>ascites</u>, hepatic or splenic lesions

* CT: <u>lung</u> <u>nodules</u>, enlarged <u>hilar lymph nodes</u>

* <u>Brain</u> <u>MRI</u>: meningeal and/or <u>basal cistern</u> <u>enhancement</u>, <u>hydrocephalus</u>, <u>tuberculoma</u>

* <u>Echocardiography</u>: <u>pericardial effusion</u>

* Treatment: See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”

![Miliary lung nodules](media/nablbepze50ldg9x3swoltqf.jpg)

Miliary lung nodules

![Lymphadenopathy and miliary lung nodules](media/j727781qsce3usd5wzd8ed4t.jpg)

Lymphadenopathy and miliary lung nodules

![Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) with gibbus deformity](media/jfolslm9ln1z3in6r00jatof.jpg)

### Tuberculous meningoencephalitis




* <u>Pathogen</u>: : <u>Mycobacterium tuberculosis</u>

* <u>Incubation period</u>: approximately 2–8 weeks

* <u>Risk factors</u>: <u>immunocompromise</u> (e.g., <u>HIV infection</u>)

* Clinical course

* Subacute course over several weeks or months

* Gradual manifestation with <u>intermittent fever</u>

* Clinical features

* Typical <u>symptoms of meningitis</u>, including <u>fever</u>, <u>headache</u>, neck stiffness, and <u>altered mental status</u> (see “Clinical features” section above for details)

* <u>Focal neurological deficits</u> (e.g., <u>hemiparesis</u>) due to hematogenous dissemination of <u>cranial arteritis</u>

* <u>Cranial nerve</u> deficits;  are most commonly seen in basal <u>meningitis</u> and predominantly involve the <u>abducens nerve</u> [[87]](/library/SqXyB_)

* Diagnostics

* <u>CSF</u> studies

* <u>CSF analysis</u> [[88]](/library/HdbKrs)

* Clear appearance with a spiderweb clot

* Variable cell count (30–300 /mm³)  [[88]](/library/HdbKrs)

* <u>Pleocytosis</u> (predominantly <u>lymphocytes</u> but also <u>granulocytes</u> and <u>mononuclear cells</u>)

* High <u>lactate</u>, protein, and <u>opening pressure</u>

* Low <u>glucose</u>

* See “<u>CSF analysis in meningitis due to atypical pathogens</u>” for comparison with other organisms.

* Presence of <u>acid-fast bacilli</u> on <u>CSF</u> <u>acid-fast staining</u>  [[88]](/library/HdbKrs)[[89]](/library/3dbSps)

* Culture is the <u>gold standard</u> for diagnosis, but results may take weeks. [[89]](/library/3dbSps)

* Analysis of <u>adenosine deaminase</u> (<u>ADA</u>) activity

* ↑↑ Activity in <u>CSF</u> of individuals with <u>tuberculous meningitis</u> compared to <u>CSF</u> of individuals with other types of <u>meningitis</u> (e.g., <u>cryptococcal</u> or <u>bacterial meningitis</u>)

* For the differentiation of tuberculous from other types of <u>meningitis</u>, combining serum and <u>CSF</u> <u>ADA</u> activity can increase <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u>. [[90]](/library/5dciqY0)

* However, reported <u>sensitivity</u> and <u>specificity</u> vary greatly in the literature; <u>confounding</u> factors include the <u>CSF</u> <u>ADA</u> cut-offs, assay types, and comorbidities (especially <u>HIV</u>). [[91]](/library/MdcMqY0)

* CT/<u>MRI</u>: possible <u>hydrocephalus</u>, basilar meningeal thickening, <u>tuberculomas</u>, <u>edema</u>, <u>infarcts</u> [[88]](/library/HdbKrs)

* Complications

* Communicating (malabsorptive) <u>hydrocephalus</u>

* <u>Pituitary gland</u> insufficiency

* Treatment

* <u>Antibiotics</u>: See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”

* Adjunctive <u>glucocorticoid</u> therapy with <u>dexamethasone</u> or <u>prednisolone</u> tapered over 6–8 weeks [[92]](/library/Dbc1Da0)





![Tuberculous meningitis](media/o9q749m7lkx5znehbl0a7ok9.jpg)

Tuberculous meningitis

![Tuberculous meningitis](media/uyolhk6mupkust04bbwhesv9.jpg)

Tuberculous meningitis




### Pericardial tuberculosis [[93]](/library/2TXTJx)[[94]](/library/fTXkJx)




* Pathophysiology

* Hematogenous spread from the site of primary infection

* Retrograde lymphatic spread from <u>hilar lymph nodes</u>

* Stages

* Stage 1: fibrinous <u>exudate</u> containing <u>neutrophils</u> and <u>mycobacteria</u>

* Stage 2: serosanguineous effusion with <u>lymphocytes</u>

* Stage 3: absorption of effusion and <u>caseating granulomas</u>

* Stage 4: scarring with calcification

* Types

* <u>Pericardial effusion</u> (rarely, <u>cardiac tamponade</u>)

* <u>Constrictive pericarditis</u>

* <u>Effusive-constrictive pericarditis</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>

* <u>Chest pain</u>

* <u>Cough</u>

* <u>Dyspnea</u>

* <u>Physical examination</u> findings: See “Clinical features” in “<u>Pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade</u>” and “<u>Pericarditis</u>.”

* Diagnostics

* <u>ECG</u>: nonspecific ST-T changes

* Imaging

* <u>Chest x-ray</u>: enlarged <u>cardiac silhouette</u> or calcification

* <u>Echocardiography</u>: effusion or diminished wall motility

* <u>Pericardiocentesis</u>

* Analysis: <u>exudative</u>, blood-stained

* Microbiology: <u>acid-fast staining</u>, <u>PCR</u>, and culture

* ↑ <u>Adenosine deaminase</u>

* Treatment

* See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”

* Consider adjunctive <u>steroids</u> only in select patients under specialist guidance (not routinely recommended). [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)

* <u>Therapeutic pericardiocentesis</u>





### Adrenal tuberculosis [[95]](/library/mfXV5x)




* Clinical features: See “<u>Adrenal insufficiency</u>.”

* Diagnostics

* CT/<u>MRI</u>: bilateral enlargement or calcification of <u>adrenal glands</u>

* See “Diagnostics” below.

* Management

* <u>Corticosteroid</u> replacement

* See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”





> [!TIP]
> <u>Rifampin</u> can precipitate an acute <u>adrenal crisis</u> in patients with undetected <u>adrenal insufficiency</u> due to tuberculosis.




### Cutaneous tuberculosis [[85]](/library/ZTXZ6x)[[96]](/library/0TXe6x)



* Classification: based on pathogenesis, morphology of the lesion, and histopathological features




| Types of <u>cutaneous TB</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Type | Pathophysiology | Clinical features | <u>Histopathology</u> features |
| <u>Exogenous</u> source of TB |  |  |  |
| <br>Primary inoculation TB (<u>tuberculous chancre</u>) | <br><br>* <u>Inoculation</u> of <u>M. tuberculosis</u> via broken <u>skin</u> or <u>mucosa</u><br><br>* Individual has no prior <u>immunity</u> against TB<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Firm and nontender <u>ulcer</u><br><br>* <u>Lymph node</u> enlargement and <u>abscess</u> formation that heals with calcification<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Granulomatous inflammation</u> with <u>caseous necrosis</u><br><br>* <u>Acid-fast bacilli</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Postprimary inoculation TB (<u>tuberculosis verrucosa cutis</u>) | <br><br>* <u>Inoculation</u> of <u>M. tuberculosis</u> via broken <u>skin</u> or <u>mucosa</u><br><br>* Individual has prior <u>immunity</u> against TB<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Hyperkeratotic</u> <u>papule</u><br><br>* No <u>lymphadenopathy</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hyperkeratosis</u><br><br> |
| <u>Endogenous</u> source of TB |  |  |  |
| Scrofuloderma | <br>* Contiguous involvement of <u>skin</u> overlying structures (e.g., <u>lymph node</u>, <u>joint</u>, <u>epididymis</u>) infected with TB<br><br> | <br>* Firm <u>nodule</u> or swelling that ulcerates to form a discharging sinus tract<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Granulomatous inflammation</u> with <u>caseous necrosis</u><br><br>* <u>Acid-fast bacilli</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Autoinoculation</u> | <br>* <u>M. tuberculosis</u> <u>inoculated</u> into orifices when secretions are expectorated (e.g., pulmonary TB) or passed (e.g., genitourinary or <u>gastrointestinal TB</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Site: <u>oral cavity</u> or <u>perineal region</u><br><br>* Tender <u>ulcers</u><br><br><br> |  |
| Hematogenous source of TB |  |  |  |
| Lupus vulgaris | <br>* Individuals previously sensitized to TB with a high degree of <u>sensitivity</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Site: face or neck<br><br>* <u>Plaques</u> or <u>nodules</u> with <u>ulceration</u> or scarring<br><br>* <u>Diascopy</u>: <u>apple jelly nodules</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Nonspecific features<br><br> |
| Tuberculosis miliaris cutis disseminata | <br>* Acute dissemination of <u>M. tuberculosis</u> from the primary focus of infection (e.g., <u>lungs</u>, <u>meninges</u>) in individuals with impaired <u>immunity</u> (e.g., as a result of <u>measles</u> or <u>HIV infection</u>)<br><br> | <br><br>* Site: trunk, thighs, buttocks, genitalia<br><br>* Widespread <u>papules</u> and crusted <u>vesicles</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Nonspecific inflammation with necrotizing <u>vasculitis</u><br><br>* <u>Acid-fast bacilli</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Tuberculous gumma (<u>metastatic tuberculous abscess</u>) | <br>* Subacute dissemination of <u>M. tuberculosis</u> in <u>immunocompromised individuals</u><br><br> | <br>* Multiple <u>skin nodules</u> that may ulcerate to form discharging sinus tract<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Granulomatous inflammation</u> with <u>caseous necrosis</u><br><br>* <u>Acid-fast bacilli</u><br><br><br> |
| Tuberculid |  |  |  |
| Variable forms | <br>* Unknown<br><br> | <br>* <u>Papules</u> or <u>nodules</u> with <u>ulceration</u> and scarring<br><br> | <br><br>* Nonspecific inflammation<br><br>* No <u>acid-fast bacilli</u><br><br><br> |





* Diagnostics: <u>skin biopsy</u> for <u>histopathology</u>, <u>acid-fast staining</u>, and culture

* Treatment: See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”





![Scrofuloderma](media/qagq6jg1nxy8wwjbygcuwrgq.jpg)

Scrofuloderma

![Dermatological tuberculosis - lupus vulgaris](media/sv4oovj7gysb4kobcszd1mum.jpg)

Dermatological tuberculosis - lupus vulgaris




### Gastrointestinal tuberculosis [[97]](/library/PTXWIx)[[98]](/library/4TX3Ix)




* Pathophysiology

* Ingestion of infected milk or <u>sputum</u>

* Hematogenous spread resulting from primary pulmonary TB

* Contiguous spread via affected <u>lymph nodes</u>

* Sites of involvement: See “Types of <u>gastrointestinal TB</u>” below.





| Types of <u>gastrointestinal TB</u> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Site of involvement | Clinical features | Diagnostics | Differential diagnosis |
| <u>Peritoneum</u> | <br><br>* Abdominal <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Ascites</u><br><br>* <u>Fever</u> and weight loss<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Abdominal <u>ultrasound</u>: <u>loculated</u> <u>ascites</u> with septations<br><br>* CT abdomen<br><br>* <u>Lymphadenopathy</u> with central <u>necrosis</u><br><br>* <u>Peritoneal</u> thickening<br><br>* <u>Ascitic fluid analysis</u><br><br>* Predominant <u>lymphocytes</u><br><br>* <u>Low SAAG ascites</u><br><br>* ↑ <u>Adenosine deaminase</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Peritoneal carcinomatosis</u><br><br>* <u>Ovarian cancer</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Esophagus</u> | <br><br>* <u>Dysphagia</u><br><br>* Retrosternal <u>chest pain</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Barium swallow</u>: stricture, <u>fistula</u>, <u>traction diverticula</u><br><br>* Endoscopy: <u>ulceration</u><br><br>* CT chest: <u>mediastinal</u> <u>lymphadenopathy</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Esophageal carcinoma</u><br><br>* <u>Sarcoidosis</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Stomach</u> | <br><br>* Epigastric <u>pain</u><br><br>* <u>Fever</u> and weight loss<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Upper GI endoscopy</u>: <u>ulceration</u>, <u>pyloric stenosis</u><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Gastric carcinoma</u><br><br>* <u>Gastric lymphoma</u><br><br>* <u>Crohn disease</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Jejunum</u> and ileocecal region | <br>* <u>Small bowel obstruction</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Abdominal <u>x-ray</u><br><br>* Dilated bowel loops with multiple <u>air fluid levels</u> (<u>intestinal obstruction</u>)<br><br>* Free air under the <u>diaphragm</u> (perforation)<br><br>* <u>Barium follow-through study</u>: multiple strictures, matted bowel loops<br><br>* CT abdomen<br><br>* Bowel wall thickening<br><br>* <u>Exophytic</u> growth in the ileocecal region<br><br>* <u>Mesenteric</u> <u>lymphadenopathy</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Crohn disease</u><br><br> |
| Colorectal | <br><br>* Abdominal <u>pain</u><br><br>* Weight loss<br><br>* Loss of appetite<br><br>* Altered bowel habits<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Barium enema</u>: strictures, <u>fistula</u><br><br>* <u>Colonoscopy</u> <br><br>* Transverse and <u>superficial</u> <u>ulcers</u> with yellow <u>exudates</u> and surrounding <u>hyperemic</u> <u>mucosa</u><br><br>* <u>Friable</u> <u>mucosal</u> <u>nodules</u><br><br>* Annular and short segment strictures (< 3 cm)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Crohn disease</u><br><br>* <u>Colon carcinoma</u><br><br>* <u>Pseudomembranous colitis</u><br><br><br> |




* Treatment

* Surgical: for <u>intestinal obstruction</u>, perforation, <u>fistula</u>, <u>abscess</u>

* Medical: See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”

Intestinal tuberculosis

![Intestinal tuberculosis (small intestine)](media/w4zztvxe4nlehdyalz0sbotq.jpg)

Intestinal tuberculosis (small intestine)




### Urogenital tuberculosis [[85]](/library/ZTXZ6x)[[99]](/library/eTXxpx)




#### Renal and urologic TB




* Pathophysiology

* Hematogenous spread of infection to the <u>kidneys</u> as a result of primary pulmonary TB that is reactivated in <u>immunosuppressed</u> states

* <u>Ureters</u> and <u>bladder</u> are infected when bacteria are excreted in urine.

* Common sites of involvement

* <u>Kidneys</u>

* <u>Ureters</u>

* <u>Bladder</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>

* Flank <u>pain</u>

* <u>Hematuria</u>

* Storage symptoms 

* Increased frequency of voiding

* <u>Nocturia</u>

* Urgency

* <u>Hypertension</u>

* <u>Recurrent UTIs</u> unresponsive to <u>antibiotic therapy</u>

* Diagnostics

* Urine examination 

* Analysis: <u>hematuria</u>, <u>sterile pyuria</u>, <u>proteinuria</u>

* Microbiology: <u>acid-fast staining</u>, <u>PCR</u>, and culture

* Imaging: CT or <u>IV urography</u>

* Renal scarring

* <u>Hydroureteronephrosis</u>

* Calcification involving the entire <u>urinary tract</u>

* Multiple ureteral strictures

* <u>Bladder</u> wall thickening and <u>fibrosis</u>

* <u>Cystoscopy</u>

* <u>Ulceration</u>

* <u>Granuloma</u>

* <u>Fibrosis</u>

* Treatment

* Medical: See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”

* <u>Ureteral stenting</u> for strictures

* <u>Surgery</u>

* Total or partial <u>nephrectomy</u>

* <u>Bladder augmentation</u>





![Putty kidney in urogenital tuberculosis](media/zy509z8eob3v4ae3dqs503k4.jpg)

Putty kidney in urogenital tuberculosis




#### Male genital tract TB




* Pathophysiology

* Hematogenous spread of infection to the <u>epididymis</u> and <u>prostate</u>

* Extension of infection from the <u>epididymis</u> to the <u>testis</u>, <u>vas deferens</u>, <u>seminal vesicles</u>, and <u>ejaculatory ducts</u>

* Common sites of involvement

* <u>Epididymis</u>

* <u>Testis</u>

* <u>Prostate</u>

* <u>Vas deferens</u>, <u>seminal vesicles</u>, and <u>ejaculatory duct</u>

* Clinical features

* Scrotal mass (can be painful or painless)

* Scrotal sinus tract with watery discharge

* <u>Infertility</u>

* Increased <u>urinary frequency</u>, <u>nocturia</u>, and <u>hematospermia</u>

* Recurrent <u>prostatitis</u> or <u>epididymitis</u> unresponsive to <u>antibiotic therapy</u>

* Diagnostics

* Urine examination

* Analysis: <u>hematuria</u>, <u>sterile pyuria</u>

* Microbiology: <u>acid-fast staining</u>, <u>PCR</u>, and culture

* Scrotal <u>ultrasound</u>

* Calcification

* <u>Hydrocele</u>

* Diffuse or nodular enlargement of the <u>epididymis</u>

* <u>Transrectal ultrasound</u>: calcification in <u>prostate</u> and <u>seminal vesicles</u>

* Treatment: See "<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”





![Tuberculous epididymitis and orchitis (urogenital tuberculosis)](media/fzomcwcojl3rzlqddv9yf1lb.jpg)

Tuberculous epididymitis and orchitis (urogenital tuberculosis)




#### Female genital tract TB [[100]](/library/UTXbJx)




* Pathophysiology: hematogenous spread of infection as a result of primary pulmonary TB that is reactivated in <u>immunosuppressed</u> states

* Common sites of involvement

* <u>Ovaries</u>

* <u>Fallopian tubes</u>

* <u>Endometrium</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>

* Menstrual irregularities

* Abdominal <u>pain</u>

* <u>Infertility</u>

* <u>Adnexal mass</u> on <u>pelvic examination</u>

* Diagnostics

* Menstrual fluid or <u>endometrial</u> <u>curettage</u> sample: <u>acid-fast staining</u>, <u>PCR</u>, and culture

* Imaging

* <u>Ultrasound</u>/CT: <u>tuboovarian abscess</u>

* <u>Hysterosalpingography</u>: occluded <u>fallopian tubes</u>, <u>hydrosalpinx</u>, calcification

* <u>Hysteroscopy</u>: adhesions and obliterated <u>uterine cavity</u>

* Treatment

* Medical: See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”

* <u>Surgery</u>: drainage of <u>tuboovarian abscess</u>





### Pott disease [[85]](/library/ZTXZ6x)




* Pathophysiology

* Hematogenous dissemination of infection to <u>vertebral bodies</u> following <u>primary TB</u>

* Infection from <u>vertebral bodies</u> spreads to the intervertebral disk, causing destruction and collapse of the disk

* Common sites of involvement: thoracic and <u>lumbar vertebrae</u>

* Clinical features

* <u>Constitutional symptoms</u>

* <u>Back pain</u>

* Spinal tenderness

* <u>Kyphosis</u>

* <u>Gibbus</u> deformity

* Neurological deficit (e.g., <u>paraplegia</u>)

* Diagnostics

* Imaging: <u>x-ray</u>, CT, or <u>MRI</u> of the <u>spine</u>

* Involvement of multiple <u>vertebrae</u>

* <u>Osteoporosis</u> of <u>vertebral</u> endplate

* Disk space narrowing

* Lytic lesions in the <u>anterior</u> <u>vertebral body</u>

* Collapse of the <u>vertebral body</u>

* Enlarged <u>psoas</u> muscle shadow (<u>psoas abscess</u>)

* <u>Spinal cord compression</u> (seen on <u>MRI</u>)

* See “Diagnostics of <u>active TB</u>.”

* Treatment

* Surgical: <u>abscess</u> drainage and/or spinal stabilization are indicated in patients with worsening or severe neurological deficits and <u>spinal instability</u>.

* Medical: See “<u>Treatment of extrapulmonary TB</u>.”





![Gibbus deformity](media/afeim3ion8xmqbvn3gekimar.jpg)

Gibbus deformity

![Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) with gibbus deformity](media/jfolslm9ln1z3in6r00jatof.jpg)

Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) with gibbus deformity

## Pathology

### Gross pathology [[3]](/library/p30Ljf)




* Multiple <u>granulomas</u> coalesce as grayish-white areas with <u>necrotic</u> centers that have a cheese-like appearance.

* Calcification and <u>fibrosis</u> are visible in healed lesions.

* <u>Ghon complex</u>  

* <u>Lung parenchyma</u>: gray-white areas of consolidation

* <u>Hilar lymph nodes</u>: <u>caseous necrosis</u>





![Caseous necrosis in lung tissue](media/nx562xaeua6whyswemeq8ei5.jpg)

Caseous necrosis in lung tissue

![Putty kidney in urogenital tuberculosis](media/zy509z8eob3v4ae3dqs503k4.jpg)

Putty kidney in urogenital tuberculosis

![Ranke complex in tuberculosis](media/c0xun0iugmw71p86lox1j64r.jpg)

Ranke complex in tuberculosis




### <u>Histopathology</u> [[3]](/library/p30Ljf)




Caseating tuberculous <u>granulomas</u> are a characteristic finding of tuberculosis, most commonly reactivation (secondary) tuberculosis.




* Center: area of <u>necrosis</u>

* Periphery: <u>epithelioid histiocytes</u> and <u>Langhans giant cells</u>





> [!NOTE]
> <u>Caseating granulomas</u> are strongly associated with tuberculosis but can also occur in infections such as <u>histoplasmosis</u> or those caused by non-tuberculous <u>mycobacteria</u> like <u>Mycobacterium avium</u>.




![Tuberculous granuloma with Langhans cells](media/ccxnj8r0b4wsvn3q34g6fafz.jpg)

Tuberculous granuloma with Langhans cells

![Miliary tuberculosis](media/e1hbkqfg98yb8a8qyi4l0fts.jpg)

Miliary tuberculosis

![Pulmonary tuberculosis](media/vuf32yexhofleat8j3src2e5.jpg)

Pulmonary tuberculosis




#### <u>Histopathology</u> of other types of tuberculosis




* Acinar nodular tuberculosis: merging of multiple epithelioid <u>granulomas</u> into macroscopically visible areas of <u>necrosis</u>

* <u>Miliary tuberculosis</u>: numerous, small, nodular foci with or without central <u>necrosis</u>

* <u>Urogenital tuberculosis</u> [[101]](/library/2iXTIB)

* Step-like progression with an initial singular focus of tuberculosis

* Gradually increasing destruction of the renal calyces

* During the end stage, the <u>kidney</u> appears to have homogeneous, sac-like collections of calcified caseous material on plain abdominal <u>x-ray</u> (known as “putty <u>kidney</u>").





![Putty kidney in urogenital tuberculosis](media/zy509z8eob3v4ae3dqs503k4.jpg)

Putty kidney in urogenital tuberculosis
