## Prevention

### Bacillus Calmette-Guérin vaccine (<u>BCG</u>) [[102]](/library/r3XfPB)




* Composition: live attenuated strain of <u>M. bovis</u>

* Administration: 0.05–0.3 mL of reconstituted <u>vaccine</u> using multiple puncture device over the deltoid region  [[103]](/library/VNdGZq0)

* Indications

* <u>Countries with a high TB burden</u>: all <u>newborns</u> at <u>birth</u> [[104]](/library/73X4PB)

* Countries with a low TB burden  [[104]](/library/73X4PB)

* Children with a negative <u>PPD TST</u> and who have come into contact with adults with untreated/inadequately treated TB or <u>drug-resistant TB</u> (if the child cannot take long-term medication for infection)

* Health care workers continually exposed to individuals with <u>drug-resistant TB</u>

* Other uses: intravesical <u>chemotherapy</u> in <u>superficial</u> <u>bladder cancer</u>

* Benefits: protects against <u>tuberculous meningitis</u> and <u>miliary TB</u> in children [[105]](/library/H3XKPB)

* Adverse effects

* Localized <u>lymphadenitis</u> and <u>abscess</u>

* <u>Disseminated TB</u> disease

* Contraindications

* <u>Immunocompromised individuals</u>

* <u>Pregnancy</u>





> [!TIP]
> The <u>BCG</u> <u>vaccine</u> is not widely used in the US and is only given to very select people in consultation with a TB expert. [[106]](/library/GecBZb0)




### <u>Disinfectants</u> active against <u>M. tuberculosis</u> [[107]](/library/t3XX4B)




* <u>Hydrogen peroxide</u>

* <u>Phenol</u>

* <u>Iodophor</u>

* <u>Chlorine-based solutions</u>

* <u>Glutaraldehyde</u>





### <u>Contact tracing</u> and postexposure management [[73]](/library/G3XBPB)




<u>Contact tracing</u> is standard practice in resource-rich countries. <u>Contact tracing</u> and treatment are usually prioritized in cases involving patients with highly infectious TB, vulnerable contacts, or high-risk exposures. [[73]](/library/G3XBPB)[[108]](/library/recfZb0)




* <u>Exposure risk</u> assessment 

* Factors that increase contagiousness of the <u>index case</u>

* Pulmonary or laryngeal TB

* Positive <u>sputum</u> smear microscopy

* Cavitary lesions on <u>chest x-ray</u>

* Untreated or inadequately treated TB

* Factors that increase contacts' vulnerability to infection 

* Age < 5 years

* Immune status: <u>HIV infection</u>, <u>corticosteroid</u> use

* Comorbid conditions

* Type of exposure: intensity, frequency, duration of exposure

* Management of contacts

* Symptomatic contacts: Obtain <u>sputum</u> smear microscopy and <u>chest x-ray</u> and manage according to results.

* Asymptomatic contacts: <u>Screening tests</u> are indicated, see “<u>Latent tuberculosis</u>” for recommendations on test selection and next steps.





> [!TIP]
> Offer <u>HIV testing</u> to all contacts if <u>HIV</u> status is unknown. [[73]](/library/G3XBPB)




> [!TIP]
> <u>Contact tracing</u> is recommended if the <u>index case</u> has pulmonary or laryngeal TB or has a positive AFB smear. [[73]](/library/G3XBPB)




#### Postexposure management in health care settings [[75]](/library/ViXGqB)




* All US health care workers are screened for <u>LTBI</u> at the beginning of their employment.

* Health care workers with previous documented <u>LTBI</u> or <u>active TB</u> do not need a <u>screening test</u> after exposure and should be evaluated if features of <u>active TB</u> develop.

---

## Special patient groups

### Management of TB in pregnant individuals [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)[[44]](/library/V3XGhB)[[109]](/library/eK1x230)




#### General [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)[[109]](/library/eK1x230)




* The diagnostic workup is the same as for nonpregnant individuals.

* Indications for <u>TB testing</u> include:

* <u>Symptoms of TB</u>

* <u>Risk factors for TB</u>

* A high likelihood of progression from <u>LTBI</u> to <u>active TB</u> (see “<u>Screening for LTBI</u>”)

* Abdominal shielding should be used to protect the fetus when performing chest <u>x-rays</u>.

* <u>Liver</u> <u>transaminases</u> should be monitored in patients receiving <u>isoniazid</u> due to an increased risk of <u>isoniazid</u>-induced <u>hepatotoxicity</u> during <u>pregnancy</u> and the <u>postpartum period</u>.





#### <u>Latent TB</u> [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)[[109]](/library/eK1x230)




* <u>Active TB</u> must to be ruled out by symptom review and chest <u>x-ray</u> before initiating treatment for <u>LTBI</u>.

* Treatment can be delayed until 2–3 months postpartum for women who are not at increased risk of developing <u>active TB</u>.

* Treatment should not be delayed in patients at high risk of developing <u>active TB</u>.





| <br>Drug regimens for treatment of LTBI in pregnant women [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
|  | Detailed regimen |
| Short regimens | <br>* <u>Isoniazid</u> and <u>rifampin</u> once daily for 3 months (abbreviation: 3HR) PLUS <u>pyridoxine</u><br><br> |
| <br>* <u>Rifampin</u> once daily for 4 months (abbreviation: 4R)<br><br> |  |
| Long regimens | <br>* <u>Isoniazid</u> once daily for 6 months (abbreviation: 6H) or 9 months (abbreviation: 9H) PLUS <u>pyridoxine</u><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> The 3HP regimen (once-weekly <u>isoniazid</u> and once-weekly <u>rifapentine</u>) is not recommended for pregnant women or women planning to become pregnant during the treatment period due to lack of data on safety during <u>pregnancy</u>. [[44]](/library/V3XGhB)




#### <u>Active TB</u> [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)[[109]](/library/eK1x230)




* Standard first-line regimen

* Intensive phase: daily <u>rifampin</u>, <u>isoniazid</u>, and <u>ethambutol</u> for 2 months

* Continuation phase: daily <u>rifampin</u> and <u>isoniazid</u> for 7 months

* <u>Adjuvant treatment</u>: <u>pyridoxine</u> to prevent <u>vitamin B<sub>6</sub> deficiency</u>

* Extrapulmonary or <u>drug-resistant TB</u>: Seek specialist advice. [[10]](/library/jec_AY0)

* Special considerations on <u>pyrazinamide</u>

* While the WHO recommends <u>pyrazinamide</u> as part of the standard treatment regimen for pregnant women, the <u>CDC</u> and <u>FDA</u> does not recommend its routine use in pregnant women due to a lack of studies in animals as well as humans. [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)[[109]](/library/eK1x230)

* If <u>pyrazinamide</u> is not used, pregnant patients with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB should be treated for at least 9 months.





> [!TIP]
> Standard first-line therapy for pregnant patients consists of 9 months with <u>isoniazid</u> and <u>rifampin</u> plus <u>ethambutol</u> during the first 2 months.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Streptomycin</u>, <u>kanamycin</u>, <u>amikacin</u>, <u>capreomycin</u>, and <u>fluoroquinolones</u> are contraindicated during <u>pregnancy</u>.




### Management during the <u>postpartum period</u> [[9]](/library/L3XwQB)[[109]](/library/eK1x230)[[110]](/library/po1L130)




* Isolation: Mothers do not need to isolate themselves from their babies after <u>birth</u> but should wear a <u>surgical mask</u>.

* <u>Breastfeeding</u> recommendations

* <u>Breastfeeding</u> should be encouraged in women receiving treatment with standard first-line agents.

* Mothers should be informed that <u>rifampin</u> can cause harmless orange discoloration of <u>breastmilk</u>.

* Exclusively breastfed <u>infants</u> should also receive prophylactic <u>pyridoxine</u> if the mother is taking <u>isoniazid</u>.





### Complications of TB during <u>pregnancy</u> [[110]](/library/po1L130)




* Maternal

* <u>Preeclampsia</u>

* <u>Eclampsia</u>

* <u>Antepartum hemorrhage</u>

* <u>Miscarriage</u>

* Fetal

* <u>Intrauterine growth restriction</u>

* <u>Preterm birth</u>

* <u>Low birth weight</u>

* Increased risk of vertical <u>HIV</u> transmission [[111]](/library/JK1sh30)

* Congenital TB (rare)  [[110]](/library/po1L130)

* <u>Perinatal</u> <u>death</u>

---
